title.en: The Inca Interrogates a Huaca: Cana-chuap Yauirca Unmasked
title.zh: 印加王質問瓦卡:揭穿卡納-查普·亞烏爾卡

region.en: Capacuyo, village of the Andes, Antisuyu (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 安蒂蘇尤安第斯村卡帕庫約(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Inca Ccapac Yupanqui wished to witness how the huacas conversed with their friends, and entered a village of the Andes called Capacuyo. The young Inca asked why they closed the doors and windows so as to leave them in the dark, and they all replied that in this way they could make the huaca come, who was the enemy of the name of God Almighty, and that there must be silence. When they had made an end of calling, it entered with a rush of wind that made them all in a cold sweat of horror. The Inca ordered doors and windows opened to see the shape of the thing they waited for with such veneration; but as soon as it was light the Devil hid its face and knew not how to answer. The dauntless Inca said: 'Tell me what you are called'; and, with much shame, it replied that its name was Cana-chuap yauirca. 'Why are you so frightened and ashamed? If you can grant children, long life, good fortune, coycollas and huacanquis, why do you stand there like a criminal without raising your eyes? I tell you that you are some false deceiver; for if you were powerful you would not be afraid nor hang down your head. I now feel that there is another Creator of all things, as my father Mayta Ccapac Ynca has told me.' The figure was ugly, with a foul smell and coarse matted hair; it fled out of the house raising shouts like thunder, and from that time all the huacas feared the Yncas, who also used the yacarcay, a rebuking formula in the name of the Creator.
summary.zh: 印加·卡帕克·尤潘琪欲親見瓦卡與其信眾對話,遂入安第斯村卡帕庫約。少年印加問眾人為何閉門塞窗、一片漆黑;眾答:如此方能召來瓦卡——它是全能上帝之名的仇敵,且須寂靜無聲。召喚完畢,那物挾一陣狂風而入,眾人嚇得冷汗直冒。印加命開門啟窗,要看清他們所虔敬恭候之物究竟何形;然而天光一亮,那魔鬼便遮住臉面,無言以對。無畏的印加喝道:「報上名來!」那物滿面羞慚,自承名為「卡納-查普·亞烏爾卡」。印加斥道:「你若真能賜子嗣、壽命、運氣、頭飾與愛情符物,為何像罪人一般垂首不敢仰視?你無非是個假騙子;你若有威能,何至於害怕?我如今確信,別有一位造物主——我父馬雅塔·卡帕克·印加早曾告我。」那形貌醜陋、氣味穢臭、毛髮蓬亂之物倉皇逃出屋外,呼叫如雷。自此諸瓦卡畏懼印加諸王;印加王亦以造物主之名誦「亞卡爾卡伊」斥逐之。

sensitivity.note: Royal huaca-interrogation episode; the Inca's monotheizing argument mirrors Salcamayhua's own Christian frame.

passages.text: It happened one day that the Ynca Ccapac Yupanqui wished to witness how the huacas conversed with their friends, so he entered the place selected, which was in a village of the Andes called Capacuyo. When the young Ynca entered among these idolaters, he asked why they closed the doors and windows so as to leave them in the dark, and they all replied that in this way they could make the huaca come, who was the enemy to the name of God Almighty, and that there must be silence. When they had made an end of calling the Devil, he entered with a rush of wind that made them all in a cold sweat of horror.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the young Ynca ordered the doors and windows to be opened, that he might know the shape of that thing for which they had waited with such veneration. But as soon as it was light the Devil hid its face, and knew not how to answer. The dauntless Ynca Ccapac Yupanqui said: 'Tell me what you are called'; and, with much shame, it replied that its name was Cana-chuap yauirca. The Ynca then said: 'Why are you so frightened and ashamed? If you can grant children, long life, good fortune, coycollas and huacanquis, why do you stand there like a criminal without raising your eyes? I tell you that you are some false deceiver; for if you were powerful you would not be afraid nor hang down your head. I now feel that there is another Creator of all things, as my father Mayta Ccapac Ynca has told me.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The figure of this devil was ugly, with a foul smell, and coarse matted hair. It fled out of the house, raising shouts like thunder; and they say that from that time all the huacas feared the Yncas; and the Yncas also used the yacarcay, in the name of the Creator, a rebuking formula beginning 'Hurinapachap hicrinpachap, cochamantarayocpa camaquimpa...'. With these words the Yncas made all the huacas tremble.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Water Touched by Tonapa: Baptism of the Infant Inca Ruca
title.zh: 托納帕所觸之水:嬰兒印加·羅卡受洗

region.en: Titicaca spring and Cuzco great square (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 的的喀喀泉與庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Inca Ccapac Yupanqui had a son by his wife Mama Corillpay-cahua, named Ynca Ruca, at whose birth there was much festivity. The Ynca sent men to search for the place called Titicaca, where the great Tonapa had arrived, and they brought water thence to pour over the infant Ynca Ruca while they celebrated the praises of Tonapa. In the spring on the top of the rocks, the water was in a basin called ccapacchama quispisutuc unu. Future Yncas caused this water to be brought in a bowl called curi-ccacca, and placed before them in the middle of the square of Cuzco, called Huacay-pata and Cusi-pata, where they did honour to the water that had been touched by Tonapa.
summary.zh: 印加·卡帕克·尤潘琪與王后瑪瑪·科里爾佩-卡瓦生子印加·羅卡,誕辰大宴。印加遣人尋訪偉大的托納帕曾到過的名為提提卡卡之地,從那裡取水,在頌揚托納帕之聲中,為嬰兒印加·羅卡灌頂。岩頂泉眼之水貯於石盆,名「卡帕克查馬-基斯皮蘇圖克-烏努」。後世印加皆命人以此水盛於「庫里-卡卡」碗中,陳於庫斯科大廣場(瓦卡伊帕塔、庫西帕塔)中央,向托納帕所觸之水致敬。

sensitivity.note: Royal baptism with Tonapa-water: the culture-hero's relic cult inside the dynasty.

passages.text: They say that this Ynca Ccapac Yupanqui had a son, by his wife Mama Corillpay-cahua, named Ynca Ruca, at whose birth there was much festivity. But the Ynca did not entirely separate himself from idolaters, as he allowed the huacas of each village to be worshipped. It is said that the Ynca sent men to search for the place called Titicaca, where the great Tonapa had arrived, and that they brought water thence to pour over the infant Ynca Ruca, while they celebrated the praises of Tonapa.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the spring on the top of the rocks, the water was in a basin called ccapacchama quispisutuc unu. Future Yncas caused this water to be brought in a bowl called curi-ccacca, and placed before them in the middle of the square of Cuzco, called Huacay-pata and Cusi-pata: where they did honour to the water that had been touched by Tonapa.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Tonapa Vihinquira Banishes the Idols to the Snowy Mountains
title.zh: 托納帕·維欣基拉逐偶像於雪山

region.en: Xauxa valley and the snowy Cordillera (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 豪哈谷與雪山脈(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: In those days the Curacas of Asillu and Hucuru told the Ynca how, in ancient times, a poor thin old man, with a beard and long hair, had come to them in a long shirt, a wise councillor in affairs of state, whose name was Tonapa Vihinquira: he had banished all the idols and hapi-ñuñu demons to the snowy mountains - to Asancata, Quiyancatay, Sallcatay and Apitosiray. The Curacas of the Huancas said this Tonapa Varivillca had also been in their land, had made a house to live in, and had banished all the huacas and hapi-ñuñus of Hatun Sausa Huanca to the snowy mountains in Pariacaca and Vallollo; before their banishment these idols had done much harm, menacing the Curacas to make them offer human sacrifices. The Ynca ordered that the house of Tonapa should be preserved, at the foot of a small hill near the river as you enter Xauxa from the Cuzco road; before coming to it there are two stones where Tonapa had turned a female huaca into stone for having fornicated with a man of the Huancas: it was called Atapymapuranutapya, and afterwards, in the time of Huayna Ccapac Ynca, the two stones declared to the people that they were huacanqui coycoylla.
summary.zh: 當時,阿西盧與庫庫魯的庫拉卡們告訴印加王:古時有一位瘦弱老者,鬚髯皆白,長髮披肩,身著長衫而來,乃是國政的明智謀士,名為托納帕·維欣基拉;他將一切偶像與哈皮紐紐惡魔逐往雪山——阿桑卡塔、基揚卡塔伊、薩爾卡塔伊、阿皮托西拉伊。萬卡人的庫拉卡亦言:這位托納帕·瓦里維爾卡曾至其地,築屋而居,將瓦通-薩烏薩-萬卡全境的瓦卡與惡魔逐往帕里亞卡卡與瓦約略的雪山;被逐之前,那些偶像為害甚烈,威逼庫拉卡獻人祭。印加王命保存托納帕之屋——在自庫斯科道入豪哈城途中河畔小山之下;近屋有兩石,乃托納帕因一女瓦卡與萬卡男子私通而將其石化者,名「阿塔皮馬普魯努塔皮亞」;至瓦伊納·卡帕克時代,二石又自稱為「瓦坎基-科伊科伊利亞」。

sensitivity.note: Huarochiri-adjacent tradition (Xauxa/Pariacaca) preserved in an Inca-focused text; tagged culture-hero against the Tonapa cluster.

passages.text: In those days the Curacas of Asillu and Hucuru told the Ynca how, in ancient times, a poor thin old man, with a beard and long hair, had come to them in a long shirt, and that he was a wise councillor in affairs of state, and that his name was Tonapa Vihinquira. They said that he had banished all the idols and hapi-ñuñu demons to the snowy mountains. All the Curacas and chroniclers also said that this Tonapa had banished all the huacas and idols to the mountains of Asancata, Quiyancatay, Sallcatay, and Apitosiray.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: When all the Curacas of the provinces of Ttahuantin-suyu were assembled in the Huacay-pata, each in his place, those of the Huancas said that this Tonapa Varivillca had also been in their land, and that he had made a house to live in, and had banished all the huacas and hapi-ñuñus in the province of Hatun Sausa Huanca to the snowy mountains in Pariacaca and Vallollo. Before their banishment these idols had done much harm to the people, menacing the Curacas to make them offer human sacrifices.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Ynca ordered that the house of Tonapa should be preserved. It was at the foot of a small hill near the river as you enter Xauxa from the Cuzco road, and before coming to it there are two stones where Tonapa had turned a female huaca into stone for having fornicated with a man of the Huancas. It was called Atapymapuranutapya, and afterwards, in the time of Huayna Ccapac Ynca, the two stones declared to the people that they were huacanqui coycoylla. In those days there were also huacanquis in the wilderness of Xauxa, and before coming to Pachacamac, and in a nest of the suyuntuy (turkey buzzard) and stones in Chincha-yunca.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Infant That Wept Blood: Yahuar-huaccac
title.zh: 泣血之嬰:亞瓦爾-瓦卡克

region.zh: 庫斯科大廣場(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The eldest son of Inca Ruca was named Yahuar-huaccac Ynca Yupanqui; his mother was Mamicay-chimpu, and at his birth there was a grand feast. The square and all the streets were filled with arches of feathers, and the house of Curicancha was entirely covered with rich plumes, both within and without. They played on eight drums and sang the ayma, torca, cayo, huallma chamayuricssa, haylli and cachra, giving thanks to the Creator. While they were all singing in the Huacay-pata, the infant wept blood, an unheard-of miracle which caused much alarm - hence the name Yahuar-huaccac Ynca. His father diligently searched for someone to interpret the meaning of this incident. In those days the hualla-huisas, cunti-huisas and cana-huisas were great sorcerers, and there assembled such a vast number of canchus, carcas, umus, uscatus and huisas that there was not room for them all in Cuzco. The Ynca did not like to confide his secrets to so many, lest the people should lose their veneration for him; so he reprehended them publicly, saying that there were many wise men but little wisdom, and dismissed them - but they returned with more liberty than before, and their idolatrous practices increased.
summary.zh: 印加·羅卡之長子名亞瓦爾-瓦卡克·印加·尤潘琪,母為瑪米凱-欽普。誕辰大宴:廣場與街衢滿懸羽拱,科里坎查神屋內外遍覆華羽;鳴八鼓,唱阿伊瑪、托爾卡、卡約、瓦爾馬·夏馬尤里克薩、阿伊利、卡克拉諸曲,謝造物主。當眾人在瓦卡伊帕塔歌唱之際,嬰兒竟泣血——聞所未聞的神蹟,舉城震恐,故名「亞瓦爾-瓦卡克」(泣血者)。其父遍尋能解此兆之人。當時瓦利亞-瓜薩、昆蒂-瓜薩、卡納-瓜薩皆大巫師;坎楚、卡爾卡、烏穆、烏斯卡圖斯、瓜薩之流雲集,庫斯科竟無處容身。印加王恐密事外洩、失眾敬畏,乃公開訓斥:「智者雖多,智慧實少」,盡數遣散;然而巫覡去而復返,行巫更無忌憚。

sensitivity.note: Name-giving birth omen; the blood-weeping infant foreshadows the dynastic tragedies later tradition attached to Yahuar Huaccac.

They played on eight drums, and sang the ayma, torca, cayo, and huallma chamayuricssa, and haylli, and cachra, giving thanks to the Creator.

passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

The Ynca did not like to confide his secrets to so many, lest the people should lose their veneration for him, so he reprehended them publicly, saying that there were many wise men but little wisdom, and he dismissed them; but these enchanters, necromancers, wizards, and witches returned with more liberty than they had had before, and their idolatrous practices increased.

title.en: The Beautiful Youth on the Rock: Stones Become Soldiers Against the Chancas
title.zh: 巖上美少年:化石成兵抗昌卡

region.en: Cuzco, besieged by the Chancas (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 被昌卡圍困的庫斯科(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: When the Hanco-Allos and Chancas besieged the city of Cuzco, the Ynca Uira-ccocha Yupanqui knew not what course to pursue and went out to arrange a peace at Yuncay-pampa. His legitimate son, Ynca Yupanqui, whom his father detested, was afflicted at the sight of his capital encompassed by an enemy; his heart was emboldened and he took the road to Cuzco. Before he arrived at Callachaca, travelling alone, he saw a very fair and beautiful youth on the top of a rock, who said: 'O son, I promise, in the name of the Creator, on whom you have called in your troubles, that he has heard you, and will give you the victory over your enemies. Fight then without fear.' Then he disappeared, and the prince felt at once emboldened and capable of command. Entering the house of arms he took out all the weapons, armed men and women, took the tupac-yauri and ccapac unancha, and unfurled the standard of the Yncas; the city became a fortress. At the first encounter the prince was knocked down by a stone from a sling and lay half insensible; then he heard a voice from heaven saying that he had not got the sceptre of tupac-yauri; he returned to the temple, took the sceptre, and returned to the battle. Meanwhile an old Ynca, Tupac Ranchiri, a priest of the Ccuricancha, set some stones in a row and fastened shields and clubs to them, so that at a distance they looked like rows of soldiers sitting down. The prince cried out to the supposed soldiers to rise; and then he saw that the stones had become men, who rose up and fought with desperate courage, assaulting the Anco-Allos and Chancas: so the prince gained the victory and beheaded the hostile chiefs Tomay-huaraca, Asto-huaraca and Huasco-Tornay Rimac. A widow named Chanan Coricoca fought valiantly in the battle like a soldier.
summary.zh: 安科-阿約與昌卡人圍困庫斯科之際,老王維拉科查·尤潘琪不知所措,竟赴永卡潘帕議和。其正妻所生、為父所惡的王子印加·尤潘琪見都城受圍,心如火焚,獨自踏上歸途。未至卡利亞查卡,他在巖頂見一極俊美的少年,少年說:「兒啊,我奉造物主之名——你在患難中所呼求者——向你應許:祂已垂聽,必賜你戰勝仇敵。奮勇而戰,勿懼!」言畢隱去,王子頓覺膽氣自生,儼然可號令三軍。他入武庫取出兵器,武裝城中男女,持圖帕克-亞烏里權杖與卡帕克軍旗,展開印加大纛;全城化為堡壘。首戰之際,王子被飛石擊倒,昏沉半死;忽聞天上有聲,責其未攜圖帕克-亞烏里權杖。他返神廟取杖再戰。此時科里坎查老祭司圖帕克-蘭奇里沿路排列石塊,縛以盾與棍,遠望如伏兵數列。王子望之,大呼「伏兵起!」——石竟成人,奮勇死戰,衝擊安科-阿約與昌卡軍。王子大捷,斬敵酋托馬伊-瓦拉卡、阿斯托-瓦拉卡、瓜斯科-托爾奈·里馬克之頭。寡婦查南·科里科卡亦如戰士般奮勇力戰。

sensitivity.note: The Chanca siege miracle, the mythic core of Pachacuti's legitimation; variants differ between Sarmiento, Cieza and Salcamayhua.

passages.text: Then the Hanco-Allos and Chancas besieged the city of Cuzco, which roused the Ynca Uira-ccocha Yupanqui from his careless ease. He knew not what course to pursue, and applied to the Hanco-Allos and Chancas; eventually he came out to arrange a peace, to Yuncay-pampa. Then his legitimate son, named Ynca Yupanqui, whom his father detested, was afflicted at the sight of his capital encompassed by an enemy. His heart was emboldened and he took the road to Cuzco, but before he arrived at Callachaca, as he travelled along the road alone, he saw a very fair and beautiful youth on the top of a rock, who said: 'O son, I promise, in the name of the Creator, on whom you have called in your troubles, that he has heard you, and will give you the victory over your enemies. Fight then without fear.' He then disappeared, and the prince felt at once emboldened and capable of command.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: On reaching his palace, he cried out, saying: 'Cuzco Ccapac pac churacllay yana pahuay may pimcanqui.' Then he entered the house of arms, and took out all the offensive and defensive weapons. At that juncture twenty Orejones arrived, his relations, sent by his father. He armed all the men and women and, entering the temple, he took the tupac-yauri and ccapac unancha, and unfurled the standard of the Yncas. The city became a fortress, and the enemy commenced the attack; but the prince had forgotten the tupac-yauri. At the first encounter, the prince Ynca Yupanqui was knocked down by a stone from a sling, and remained half insensible. Then he heard a voice from heaven saying that he had not got the sceptre of tupac-yauri. So he went back to the temple and took the sceptre, and returned to the battle, encouraging the captains and soldiers to fight.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Meanwhile an old Ynca, a near relation of the prince's father, named Tupac Ranchiri, who was a priest of the Ccuricancha, set some stones in a row, and fastened shields and clubs to them, so that they might look at a distance like rows of soldiers sitting down. The prince, looking out for succour from his father, saw these rows from a distance, and cried out to the supposed soldiers to rise, as his men were on the point of yielding. The Chancas continued the attack with increased fury, and then the prince saw that the stones had become men, and they rose up and fought with desperate courage and skill, assaulting the Anco-Allos and Chancas; so the prince gained a victory, and followed the enemy to Quizachilla, where he beheaded the chiefs of the hostile army, named Tomay-huaraca, Asto-huaraca, and Huasco-Tornay Rimac. They say that a widow named Chanan Coricoca fought valiantly in the battle like a soldier.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: He Takes the Name of His Brother's Slayer: Pachacuti
title.zh: 他取了殺弟者之名:帕查庫提

region.zh: 科利亞蘇尤瓦伊拉-坎恰(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Inca Urcu, the natural son to whom Viracocha Inca had renounced the kingdom in his lifetime, undertook the conquest of Colla-suyu; he passed through the country of the Caviñas taking with him the statue of Manco Ccapac to secure good fortune, but was defeated and killed at Huana-calla by the hand of Yamqui Pachacuti, the chief of Huayra-Cancha. After his victory over the Chancas, Inca Yupanqui followed the enemy to Andahuayllas, returned to Cuzco, and undertook the conquest of Colla-suyu; among the chiefs who submitted was the famous Yamqui-Pachacuti, whom the prince thanked for the death of Inca Urcu, his brother; and the prince took his name and added it to his own, which became Pachacuti Ynca Yupanqui. He conquered all the land of the Colla-suyu and invaded the provinces of the Chayas and Caravayas, where he destroyed a famous idol.
summary.zh: 維拉科查生前將王位讓與庶子印加·烏爾庫。烏爾庫率大軍征科利亞蘇尤,攜曼科·卡帕克神像以求勝運,然在瓦納-卡利亞為瓦伊拉-坎恰之酋雅姆基·帕查庫提所敗殺。王子印加·尤潘琪大破昌卡後,追敵至安達瓦伊利亞斯,返庫斯科,繼而征科利亞蘇尤;來降諸酋中,即有殺其兄烏爾庫的雅姆基-帕查庫提。王子謝其弒兄之功,並取其名加於己名之上,遂稱「帕查庫提·印加·尤潘琪」。他征服科利亞蘇尤全境,又侵查亞斯與卡拉瓦亞斯諸省,毀其著名神像。

sensitivity.note: Name-taking episode; Salcamayhua records the awkward fact that 'Pachacuti' was the name of the brother-slayer, against later idealized versions.

passages.text: He had a natural son named Ynca Urcu, to whom he renounced the kingdom during his life time. This Ynca Urcu undertook the conquest of Colla-suyu with a great army... He passed through the country of the Caviñas, taking with him the statue of Manco Ccapac, to secure good fortune for himself. But he was defeated and killed at Huana-calla, by the hand of Yamqui Pachacuti, the chief of Huayra-Cancha.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Ynca Yupanqui followed the enemy as far as Andahuayllas; and, on his return to Cuzco, he undertook the conquest of Colla-suyu; and other provinces submitted peaceably. Among them was that of the famous chief Yamqui-Pachacuti, whom the prince thanked for the death of Ynca Urcu, his brother. And the prince took his name and added it to his own, which became Pachacuti Ynca Yupanqui. He conquered all the land of the Colla-suyu, and invaded the provinces of the Chayas and Caravayas, where he destroyed a famous idol.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Amaru of Pachatusan: A Half-League Serpent and Comets of Fire
title.zh: 帕查圖桑之阿瑪魯:半萊格巨蛇與火焰彗星

region.en: Mountain of Pachatusan, above Cuzco (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 庫斯科上方帕查圖桑山(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: At Puma-cancha, where his eldest legitimate son Amaru Yupanqui was born, news arrived to Pachacuti of a miracle at Cuzco: a yauirca or amaru, a ferocious creature half a league long and two and a half brazas wide, with ears, eye-teeth, and a beard, had come forth from the mountain of Pachatusan and entered the lake of Quichuipay. Then two sacacas (comets) of fire came out of Ausancata, one going towards Arequipa and another towards snowy mountains near Huamanca: they were described as animals with wings, ears, a tail, and four legs, with many spikes on their backs, appearing from a distance to be made of fire. Pachacuti set out for Cuzco, where he found his father very old and infirm.
summary.zh: 帕查庫提留駐普馬-坎恰(長子阿瑪魯·尤潘琪誕生之地)時,得庫斯科神異之報:一條「亞烏爾卡」(阿瑪魯)——兇猛巨獸,長半萊格、寬兩布拉薩半,有耳、有獠牙、有鬚——自帕查圖桑山出,入基丘伊帕湖。又有兩顆火質「薩卡卡斯」(彗星)自奧桑卡塔出,一奔阿雷基帕,一奔瓦曼卡附近雪山;狀如有翼四足之獸,有耳有尾,背生尖刺,遠望如烈火所成。帕查庫提遂啟程回庫斯科,見其父維拉科查已衰老不堪。

sensitivity.note: Omen cycle around Pachacuti's return; the amaru serpent and fire-comets read as dynastic portents.

passages.text: In Puma-cancha his eldest legitimate son was born, named Amaru Yupanqui, and he rested there for some days. Here the news arrived of a miracle at Cuzco. A yauirca or amaru, a ferocious creature, half a league long and two brazas and a half wide, with ears, eye-teeth, and a beard, had come forth from the mountain of Pachatusan, and entered the lake of Quichuipay.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then two sacacas (comets) of fire came out of Ausancata, and went towards Arequipa; and another went towards some snowy mountains near Huamanca. They were described as animals with wings, ears, a tail, and four legs, with many spikes on their backs; and from a distance they appeared to be made of fire. So Pachacuti Ynca Yupanqui set out for Cuzco, where he found that his father, Uira-ccocha Ynca Yupanqui, was now very old and infirm.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: White Vicuña Wool and Shorn Women: The Mourning for Viracocha Inca
title.zh: 白駝馬毛與剪髮之婦:維拉科查·印加之喪

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: When his father died, the mourning was vicuña wool of a white colour; and the soldiers were ordered to carry the body of the old man, with his arms and insignia, through the city, singing a war-song and bearing their shields and clubs, their llaca-chuquis, chasca-chuquis, suruc-chuquis. The women came forth in another procession, with their hair shorn, and dressed in black, and their faces blackened, flogging themselves with quichuas and coyas, secsec, sihuicas. They say that these women mourned for a whole week, and sought for the body of the dead Ynca.
summary.zh: 其父既歿,舉喪以白色駝馬毛為服;士兵奉命抬老王遺體,攜其兵甲印信,持盾執棍——拉卡-楚基、查斯卡-楚基、蘇魯克-楚基——唱戰歌巡行全城。婦人另成一隊,剪髮縞衣,面塗黑色,以基丘阿與科亞、塞克塞克、西瓜卡斯自笞其身。相傳婦人哀慟整整一週,遍尋先王遺體。

sensitivity.note: Royal mourning description from Salcamayhua's dynastic narrative.

passages.text: When his father died, the mourning was vicuña wool of a white colour; and the soldiers were ordered to carry the body of the old man, with his arms and insignia, through the city, singing a war-song and bearing their shields and clubs, their llaca-chuquis, chasca-chuquis, suruc-chuquis. The women came forth in another procession, with their hair shorn, and dressed in black, and their faces blackened, flogging themselves with quichuas and coyas, secsec, sihuicas. They say that these women mourned for a whole week, and sought for the body of the dead Ynca.

title.en: The Eagle and the Serpent of Canacuay

region.en: Anca-pirca terrace, province of the Caviñas (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡維尼亞斯省安卡-皮爾卡階地(象徵性標記)

source.work: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti-yamqui Salcamayhua, 'An Account of the Antiquities of Peru', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The Capacuyos sent a poor man with hultis (clay pots for llipta), who gave Pachacuti a blow on the head with the intention of killing him. The man was tortured and confessed he was a Caviña of the Quiquijanas sent to kill the Ynca at the request of the Capacuyos, whose Curaca was Apu Calama Yanqui: nearly 20,000 of them, besides women and children, were put to death, for they had tried to murder the Ynca by advice of their huaca Canacuay. Then the Ynca's second son Tupac Ynca Yupanqui was born, and the Ynca undertook the conquest of the Antisuyus with 100,000 men. But the huaca of Canacuay sent forth fire, and stopped the passage with a fierce serpent which destroyed many people. The Ynca raised his eyes to heaven and prayed for help with great sorrow, and a furious eagle descended, and, seizing the head of the serpent, raised it on high and then hurled it to the ground. In memory of this miracle the Ynca ordered a snake to be carved in stone on the wall of a terrace in this province, which was called Anca-pirca.
summary.zh: 卡帕庫約人遣一貧漢,攜裝里普塔的陶罐,乘間重擊帕查庫提頭部,欲殺之。刑訊之下,其人自認乃基基哈納的卡維尼亞人,奉卡帕庫約人之請來刺印加王——其酋為阿普·卡拉馬·揚基。於是卡帕庫約男女老幼近二萬人盡遭處死,因其曾依其瓦卡「瓦納庫瓦」之謀試圖弒王。其後印加次子圖帕克·尤潘琪誕生;印加王率十萬大軍征安蒂蘇尤。然而瓦納庫瓦瓦卡噴出火焰,並遣一條兇蛇堵截隘道,噬殺甚眾。印加王悲慟仰望上天求援,一隻猛鷹撲下,攫住蛇頭,高舉而擲之於地。為誌此神蹟,印加王命人在該省一處階地牆上鑿石為蛇,其地名「安卡-皮爾卡」。

sensitivity.note: Serpent-guardian huaca and eagle miracle; the massacre of the Capacuyos is recorded as given, critically.

passages.text: At that time they say that the Capacuyos sent a poor man with hultis (clay pots in which they keep llipta), who gave Pachacuti Ynca a blow on the head with the intention of killing him. The man was tortured, and confessed that he was a Caviña of the Quiquijanas, and that he had come to kill the Ynca at the request of the Capacuyos. So the Ynca ordered the province of the Caviñas to be laid waste; but they said that the fault was not theirs, but the Capacuyos, whose Curaca was Apu Calama Yanqui, and who numbered near 20,000 men, besides women and children. They were all put to death. They say that they tried to murder the Ynca, by advice of their huaca, Canacuay.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Salcamayhua, Antiquities of Peru (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Ynca's second son was born, named Tupac Ynca Yupanqui; and the Ynca undertook the conquest of the Antisuyus with 100,000 men. But the huaca of Canacuay sent forth fire, and stopped the passage with a fierce serpent which destroyed many people. The Ynca raised his eyes to heaven and prayed for help with great sorrow, and a furious eagle descended, and, seizing the head of the serpent, raised it on high and then hurled it to the ground. In memory of this miracle the Ynca ordered a snake to be carved in stone on the wall of a terrace in this province, which was called Anca-pirca.
